comment.value: This paper outlines the molecular pose generation, guided by templates. This is an important task in computer aided drug-design, where given a known co-crystallized ligand:target complex, the aim is to generate new candidate ligands informed by this information. The authors present a two-tiered approach to this: one for generation and the second for refinement. While reviewers critiqued the initial submission for unclear statement of design choices and limited ablations among other things, following the rebuttal and discussion period, all reviewers agreed that this work passes the acceptance threshold since it presents a first two-tiered and neural approach to the task at hand, and due to the modularity, it is likely that the individual components of the model can be adopted in other contexts.
Thank you for your feedback. We appreciate your thoughtful comments throughout the review process.

Thank you for your thoughtful feedback. Please find our responses to your additional comments below.

> Q1.2. It would be still interesting to look at the PB-validity numbers.

Thank you for this relevant suggestion. Below are the updated PB-validity numbers after applying the clash optimization:
| Method     | Clash Optimization | PB-valid & RMSD < 2Å | RMSD < 2Å |
|------------|--------------------|-----------------------|-----------|
| FMA-PO     | No             | 51%                   | 72%       |
| FMA-PO     | Yes              | 59%                   | 71%       |
| FMA-PO+    | No             | 68%                   | 80%       |
| FMA-PO+    | Yes              | 72%                   | 79%       |

Some poses remain non PB-valid due to a few tetrahedral chirality errors (the specified tetrahedral chirality in the predicted molecule is not the same as in the true molecule). Moreover, despite the clash optimization, residual clashes with the protein still exist in some cases, as shown in Table 3, although their number has decreased. Overall, the reviewer’s suggestion led to an improvement in PB-valid pose quality (e.g., from 51% to 59% in FMA-PO). Nonetheless, there is still room for PO improvement, and future work will focus on better handling of protein-ligand clashes, and fixing chirality-related issues.

---
> Q5. I think in scenarios where the protein structure is not available you would also not have 3D coordinates of the reference ligand. I can hardly imagine a situation where you would know 3D coordinates of the reference ligand but would not have access to the 3D pocket information (or would decide to ignore the available protein 3D information).

We agree that in most practical scenarios, if an experimental 3D structure of a reference ligand is available, the 3D structure of the protein binding pocket is also accessible. However, in some situations, active ligands are known, but experimental 3D of the target is not (e.g. phenotypic hits). In such cases, a plausible modeled 3D conformation of the ligand can support ligand-based shape/pharmacophore virtual screening or be coupled with a generative method for de novo design [1].

---

References

[1] Bolcato, G., Heid, E., & Bostrom, J. (2022). On the value of using 3D shape and electrostatic similarities in deep generative methods. Journal of chemical information and modeling, 62(6), 1388-1398.

Thanks for the relevant questions, please find our responses below. 

> (1) Does this result mean FMA can not be used as a standalone ligand alignment tool?

In terms of RMSD, FMA is the best-performing method, as shown in Table 1. However, it is not optimal in terms of strain energy (Table 1 in our response to reviewer Pn5y). This is expected: FMA is an all-atom Flow Matching (FM) model trained to minimize RMSD, not internal energy. Small coordinate deviations that barely affect RMSD can incur large energy penalties, leading to mild chemical distortions (e.g., slightly stretched/compressed bonds, non-planar aromatics). Consequently, FMA should be followed by all-atom energy refinement. This is precisely why we introduce PO, which reduces strain energy while improving the alignment obtained by FMA (Table 1 in our response to reviewer Pn5y). In practice, FMA is an excellent initializer for alignment, but not a standalone tool when chemically realistic geometries are required.

> (2) How does it happen that FMA has "all-atom distortions", but performs best in Table 2?

FMA tops Table 2 because it delivers the most accurate global alignment before any refinement. 
The “all-atom distortions” we mention are local (slightly stretched bonds, non-planar rings, etc.). They barely affect the overall RMSD, so FMA can still achieve the best starting pose. These local defects, however, raise the strain energy, which we subsequently remove with our PO all-atom optimizer while improving the alignment.

> (3) As far as I know, FitDock performed binding conformation refinement, so why couldn't it fix all-atom distortions?

Although FitDock includes a refinement step, it optimizes the AutoDock Vina interaction scoring function, which accounts for binding interactions but does not include the ligand’s internal energy (see the Binding Conformation Refinement section in the FitDock paper).
The conformation generated by FMA may not be well suited as a starting point for torsion-based methods like FitDock or Vina. This likely explains the poor performance observed in Table 4 for FMA+FitDock and FMA+Vina combinations.

We thank the reviewer for the feedback and evaluation of our method. We
provide detailed answers in the following. To clarify the FM
architecture and conditioning, we prepared a detailed FMA pipeline
figure, which will be included in the final manuscript (can’t include
figure here due to NeurIPS policy).
***
> Q1 : Could you report the actual distributions, e.g., the CDF showing how many ligands have an RMSD of < x? 

Per the suggestion, we report RMSD CDFs in
Table 1; the corresponding plot will appear
in the final manuscript.
***
### Table 1 : Cumulative distribution of RMSD values: percentage of molecules with RMSD below different thresholds.


| **Method** | \<0.5 Å(%) | \<1.5 Å(%) | \<2.0 Å(%) | \<3.0 Å(%) | \<4.0 Å(%) | \<8.0 Å(%) |
|:-----------|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|
| FMA        |     0      |     40     |     60     |     90     |     90     |    100     |
| FMA-PO     |     10     |     50     |     70     |     80     |     90     |    100     |
| FMA-PO+    |     10     |     60     |     80     |     90     |     90     |    100     |
| FitDock    |     0      |     40     |     50     |     70     |     70     |    100     |
| LSalign    |     0      |     30     |     50     |     80     |     80     |    100     |
| ROSHAMBO   |     0      |     30     |     50     |     70     |     80     |    100     |
| Vina       |     0      |     40     |     50     |     60     |     70     |     90     |
| rDock      |     0      |     20     |     30     |     50     |     50     |     80     |


***

> Q2 : It was not particularly clear to me how the flow matching sampling works in detail. From figure 2 it seems like the crystallized ligand is used as a conditioning of the NNET that is present across all t. However, if this is the case, what target distribution are you using during training?

**(i) Training dataset construction.** Training requires well‑defined
(template, query) pairs with ground truth alignment. Each pair consists
of two different ligands co‑crystallized with the same protein (same
binding site). Ground‑truth alignment is defined via protein
superposition: we compute a rigid‑body alignment between the two
receptors (Kabsch on C$_\alpha$ of the binding site), and apply the
resulting rotation/translation to all atoms of the query complex. This
places both complexes into a common coordinate frame. The transformed
coordinates of the query ligand define the target pose for training,
while the transformed coordinates of the template ligand serve as
conditioning. Please see section 3.4 for training set construction
details.

**(ii) Conditioning on the template ligand.** Conditioning occurs at two
levels (See Appendix A3):

- \(a\) The encoder processes a joint graph over the 2D molecular graphs
  of the query and the template, including cross-ligand edges. This
  joint representation allows the query encoding to attend to the
  chemical and topological features of the template.

- \(b\) The vector‑field network processes the fixed 3D coordinates of
  the template along with the current (noisy) coordinates of the query
  at time $t$ when predicting velocity $v_t$ of the query.

**(iii) Flow‑matching training.** We minimize the following objective :
$$
\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}\_{t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1),\\\ \mathbf{x}\sim\rho\_t} \big\\\|\mathbf{v}\_\theta(t,\mathbf{x}\mid \text{template})-\mathbf{v}\_t(\mathbf{x})\big\\\|^2
$$
where $\mathbf{v}\_\theta(t,\mathbf{x}\mid \text{template})$ is the
learned velocity used to denoise the query at time $t$ conditioned on
the template, and $v\_t$ the analytical velocity mapping the initial
distribution to the target one:
$$
\mathbf{v}\_t(\mathbf{x}) =  \mathbf{x}\_1-\mathbf{x}\_0  + \frac{1-2t}{2\sqrt{t(1-t)}} \mathbf{z},
\quad \mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}),$$ with $\mathbf{x}\_0$ a
harmonic prior conformation of the query and $\mathbf{x}\_1$ the query’s
crystal ground‑truth pose.

**(iv) Sampling.** At inference we draw an initial harmonic pose of the
query $\mathbf{x}\_0$ centered on the template, and integrate the learned
veolcity with a deterministic Euler solver from $t{=}0\to1$ (30
uniform steps), yielding the final pose at $t{=}1$:
$$
\mathbf{x}\_{t+\Delta t} = \mathbf{x}\_t +\\mathbf{v}\_\theta\big(t,\mathbf{x}\_t \mid \text{template}\big) \Delta t
$$
***
> Q3 : How does each part of your method (i.e., flow matching and refinement) contribute to the overall results? Did you test whether samples generated with your flow matching also improves other energy-based refinement algorithms such as VINA?

We performed ablation studies on AlignDockBench to quantify the
contribution of each stage:

1.  **FMA’s contribution (Table 2):**
    We generated 10 candidate poses per method (FMA, RDKit‑centroid,
    Vina, LS‑align, FitDock‑LB), applied PO to each, and selected the
    top‑ranked pose. The RDKit‑centroid baseline places a random
    conformer at the binding‑site center. FMA+PO consistently yields the
    lowest RMSD among all alternatives, indicating that FMA is the best
    initialization strategy for PO and that its accuracy is crucial.

2.  **PO’s contribution (Table 3):**
    PO consistently reduced RMSD when applied to top poses from other
    methods, supporting its general effectiveness as a refinement stage.
    PO also improves chemical plausibility and geometrical validity (see response to reviewer Pn5y - Table 1, 2).

3.  **FMA followed by other optimizers (Table 4):**
    Using FitDock, Vina or rDock on FMA outputs degraded performance, likely
    due to their inability to correct all-atom distortions introduced by
    FMA. In contrast, PO is designed for full atomic refinement and is
    better suited to correct such issues.

We will include these results and the related discussion in the revised
manuscript.

> Q.4 : How is pharmocophoric complementarity between protein and ligand computed? For example, a hydrogen bond between protein and ligand would be represented by a pair of "complementary" pharmacophores. The concept of pharmacophoric complementarity in our pose optimization
(PO) process is implemented by maximizing the overlap between
complementary pharmacophoric Gaussians in the presence of an internal
energy term and a steric clash penalty. Specifically, the Hydrogen Bond
Donors (HBD) includes an explicit hydrogen atom, and the Hydrogen Bond
Acceptors (HBA) is a complementary features, as Cation and Anion
features are.

In our PO approach, the geometry of hydrogen bonds is oriented by the
combined effect of the three key components:

- **Pharmacophoric Gaussian placement:** A Gaussian sphere labeled as an
  HBD is placed on the hydrogen atom of a donor group. The PO
  optimization maximizes the overlap between this donor Gaussian and a
  complementary HBA Gaussian from the pocket (via the $S_{\text{PTS}}$
  term), reducing the donor–acceptor distance and favoring the
  near-linear X–H$\cdots$X geometry.

- **Internal energy regularization:** An internal energy term based on
  GAFF2 is used in the PO loss and maintains chemically plausible
  geometries, in particular the C–X–H angles, and the distance between the heavy atoms.

- **Steric clash penalty:** The  $-S\_{\text{PTS}}$ term between ligand and pocket penalizes excessive Gaussian overlap, preventing the system from favoring unrealistic geometries.

The protein pocket provides valuable structural information and is used
in PO when available. However, in many real-world drug discovery
settings, such as ligand-based virtual screening or *de novo*
generation, the protein structure is not always known or used. To
support these scenarios, we designed FMA and FMA-PO to remain effective
without pocket input. The *optional* label reflects this flexibility and
broad applicability across both structure-based and ligand-based
workflows.

The weights of the loss terms were empirically tuned using a validation
set of ten diverse protein–ligand complexes from the training data. For
each term—shape similarity, pharmacophoric complementarity, steric clash
penalty, and internal energy regularization—we explored multiple
weightings. The final values were chosen based on convergence behavior,
pose quality, and RMSD across the validation set.

summary.value: This paper proposes FMA-PO, a two-step method for ligand 3D pose prediction using flow matching for initial alignment and differentiable optimization for pose refinement. It introduces a new benchmark (AlignDockBench) and shows competitive results compared to docking and alignment baselines.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Pros:

* Tackles an important problem in drug design: predicting ligand poses in the presence of a known co-crystallized template. 
* Provides a new benchmark dataset, which could be valuable to the community. 
* The proposed method shows good experimental results on challenging cases with low template similarity.

Cons:
*  The FMA module is trained without incorporating protein structural information, yet the benchmark labels are derived from co-crystallized complexes that inherently involve protein context. This discrepancy could introduce bias or limit generalizability. A discussion of this mismatch—and potentially experiments adding protein context into FMA—would be useful.
*  The proposed method involves two stages: ligand alignment and pose optimization. However, the contribution of each stage to the overall performance is not quantified. I encourage the authors to include ablation experiments to isolate the benefit of each stage.

questions.value:
My main concern is on the insufficient analysis of two components: the alignment module and the pose optimization module.

From my perspective, a key open question is whether the proposed neural network-based ligand alignment outperforms traditional alignment strategies. It would be helpful to compare with classical or widely used alignment methods, such as:
* KCOMBU [1]
* The shape alignment algorithm used in FitDock [2]
* Schrödinger’s shape-based alignment approach [3]
Even if direct benchmarking is not feasible for all of them, some discussion or rationale for the neural approach (e.g., accuracy vs. speed trade-offs) would strengthen the paper.

To further assess the value of the proposed pose optimization (PO) stage, a simple but informative experiment would be to use the alignment generated by the current method, followed by pose refinement using FitDock's optimization network (or vice versa). This would help evaluate the robustness and modularity of each stage.

Misc:
*  The paper mentions modules like MHAwithEdgeBias and PointSetAttentionwithEdgeBias but doesn’t explain them in enough detail. Brief architectural or pseudo-code descriptions would help.
*  Some hyperlinks in the manuscript are invalid or incomplete. Please check and fix them for clarity.
*  A relevant citation is missing: the authors should consider citing GroupBind [4], which is very relevant to template-guided modeling.

Overall:

While the direction of the work is promising, the current version lacks sufficient analysis of its components and omits comparisons to standard baselines. The contributions are somewhat difficult to isolate. With additional analysis and explanation, I would be more inclined to support acceptance in the future.

summary.value: The paper introduces a two-stage framework called FMA-PO, which combines a flow-matching-based model for template-guided ligand pose generation with a differentiable pose refinement module. The method aligns a 2D query molecule to a 3D reference ligand using flow matching, and then refines it based on shape, pharmacophore, internal energy, and optional pocket information. The authors release AlignDockBench, a benchmark dataset specifically for template-based pose generation, containing 369 protein-ligand pairs with co-crystallized templates. This is a valuable contribution on its own, as template-based evaluations are often missing in public datasets.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
- The model design is clean and modular. The use of a harmonic prior and graph-based encoding of atom and fragment features allows smooth integration into the FM formulation. This feels like a natural extension of recent works like FlowDock and DiffDock, but with the added benefit of using template ligands instead of receptor pockets.

- The differentiable optimization step is thoughtfully designed. It balances pharmacophore similarity, shape matching, and internal energy terms, which are all differentiable with respect to coordinates. The ability to optionally incorporate protein pocket info is a nice touch and makes the model flexible across use cases.

- Empirical results on AlignDockBench show consistent improvements over several baselines, including FitDock, LS-align, and traditional docking tools like Vina and rDock. The paper reports both mean RMSD and % of poses under 2Å, which are standard and appropriate.

- The improvement in low-similarity and high-flexibility regimes is especially noteworthy. Most alignment tools tend to fail in these settings, and the method's robustness here makes it practically useful.

- The FMA-PO+ variant, where all samples are refined before ranking, offers stronger performance but at the cost of runtime. This tradeoff is acceptable, and it's good that the authors report both variants.

- One thing that's missing is a comparison to recent flow-based or diffusion-based methods like HarmonicFlow or SE(3)-FM. These are the most relevant generative baselines for 3D generation, and even a small subset comparison would help contextualize FMA's performance.

- The use of a Vina-based score in the final scoring function (Sscore) might be a bit confusing, given that Vina was also used as a baseline. It would be good to clarify if this introduces any advantage or bias when comparing methods.

- The paper notes that all runs were done on T4 GPUs and provides runtime comparisons, which is appreciated. Still, there's no mention of how model performance scales with ligand size, does runtime blow up with more rotatable bonds or heavy atoms?

- The benchmark design seems solid, but it would be great to release a few more challenging cases or outlier visualizations, especially where the method succeeds but others fail. This would highlight the strengths of the alignment stage more clearly.

summary.value: This paper introduces a FM-based method for template-based ligand docking. First, authors formulate the ligand conformer generation task conditioned on the template 3D structure with flow matching. Next, authors propose the pose optimisation (PO) algorithm that refines the generated pose using shape and colour similarity and additional pocket constraints. Authors evaluate the method on a newly curated  benchmark AlignDockBench and show that the proposed method outperforms other structure-based and ligand-based approaches.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
- Strengths: clear formulation and presentation, new benchmark, good results (in terms of RMSD).
- Weaknesses: apparently low quality of the generated structures and insufficient ablation studies (see Questions).

questions.value:
1. My main concern is about the quality of the generated molecules. While I agree that the ultimate metric in this task is RMSD, I believe that the high quality of the designed conformations is the necessary condition to meet - even before computing RMSD. Besides, the proposed PO has multiple objectives some of which are directly connected to the molecule quality (i.e., steric clashes and strain energies). Based on this, I have two comments:
 - (1.1) In my opinion, the work would benefit a lot from an additional subsection where the authors focus on the quality metrics of the generated poses: i.e. what are the distributions of strain energies for FMA and FMA-PO? how do they compare with the reference molecules and with other methods? same for steric clashes. For future work I would also recommend to look at GenBench3D (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04424) - I find it very neat for measuring the 3D quality of generated molecules.
 - (1.2) I see that in the Appendix authors report PB-validity values and they are not very high. I would suggest to focus on these problems and incorporate additional terms in the refinement objective that would improve these values.

2. The proposed PO consists of four terms but I found ablation studies only for the pocket term. I would suggest to do ablation studies for all four to clearly understand the importance of each of them.

3. How strong is contribution of S_Vina in the final S_Score?

4. How is pharmocophoric complementarity between protein and ligand computed? For example, a hydrogen bond between protein and ligand would be represented by a pair of "complementary" pharmacophores. But depending on the relative orientation of these pharmacophores a hydrogen bond may or may not exist.

5. Why is protein pocket input always labeled as optional? To me pocket looks like an essential component for this task.

6. How were the weights in Table S2 tuned?

summary.value: The authors introduce a two-step approach for molecular pose generation. Given a template (such as the crystalized version of a ligand), they use flow matching to generate an initial guess for conformations. In a second step, this is then optimized with a differentiable approach that includes biochemical properties (such as the energy) and can also include the binding pocket if the aim is docking. This approach can be seen as a hybrid of a structure-based and ligand-based method. They also introduce a benchmark for template-based docking with broader and more realistic settings.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
The ideas presented in the paper are discussed and demonstrated in detail and an extensive appendix is provided containing a variety of technical details. Generally, the paper is well written and easy to follow, however it took some time to understand the specific flow matching setup they were using and how the model is conditioned on the template. Improving figure 1 might go a long way in making the paper more accessible and easier to digest.

The main issue I see with the paper is that it is lacking a bit of focus. They introduce three (relatively independent) parts: A flow matching model, a refinement procedure, and the benchmark dataset. While the flow matching part itself is not particularly novel, combining it with the refinement procedure demonstrates improvements is. However, it is not particularly clear / discussed enough how much the flow matching vs refinement contributes to the results. Discussing this in more detail (maybe both parts are equally needed), could help distilling the focus of the work.

Apart from that, the authors have discussed their work in detail and especially the discussion in section 5 helps to put the results into context.

questions.value:
1. The authors reported standard deviations in their main results (table 1), however, they are often quite large and it is not particularly clear whether their method is actually better. It seems like FMA-PO+ is more robust and shows to have a smaller standard deviation. Could you report the actual distributions, e.g., the CDF showing how many ligands have an RMSD of < x? This would make it easier to compare the methods and quantify the results. 

2. It was not particularly clear to me how the flow matching sampling works in detail. From figure 2 it seems like the crystallized ligand is used as a conditioning of the NNET that is present across all $t$. However, if this is the case, what target distribution are you using during training? 

3. How does each part of your method (i.e., flow matching and refinement) contribute to the overall results? Did you test whether samples generated with your flow matching also improves other energy-based refinement algorithms such as VINA? 

4. In Appendix D.5.1 you compared your method with and without pocket information. In table S5, it seems like FMA-PO with pocket seems to perform worse when having pocket information. I would have assumed the score to be better. Could you explain or do you have an intuition for this discrepancy?

limitations.value: For the most part, the authors have adequately discussed the limitations of their work. However, I would have like more discussion about the runtime and whether the performance could be improved for the method to be suitable for large screens.

final_justification.value:
In the initial submission, the paper lacked a clear focus. It was difficult to assess which components of the proposed method were driving the observed improvements, or whether all parts were necessary. Additionally, their main results just included RMSD values with certain cutoffs, without any cumulative distributions reported. This made it challenging to fully evaluate the performance.


However, with thanks to the comments from the authors, the new results now include additional comparisons, including ablations with existing methods such as VINA or more detailed results. The authors have also adequately addressed critical points raised by the other reviewers, such as the addition of steric clashes which is important to study.

Given these improvements and the thorough responses to the key concerns raised during the review process, I am increasing my score to 4. I believe the paper is now above the acceptance threshold.

title.value: Template-Guided 3D Molecular Pose Generation via Flow Matching and Differentiable Optimization

abstract.value: Predicting the 3D conformation of small molecules within protein binding sites is a key challenge in drug design. When a crystallized reference ligand (template) is available, it provides geometric priors that can guide 3D pose prediction. We present a two-stage method for ligand conformation generation guided by such templates. In the first stage, we introduce a molecular alignment approach based on flow-matching to generate 3D coordinates for the ligand, using the template structure as a reference. In the second stage, a differentiable pose optimization procedure refines this conformation based on shape and pharmacophore similarities, internal energy, and, optionally, the protein binding pocket. We introduce a new benchmark of ligand pairs co-crystallized with the same target to evaluate our approach and show that it outperforms standard docking tools and open-access alignment methods, especially in cases involving low similarity to the template or high ligand flexibility.

Deep learning (e.g., architectures, generative models, optimization for deep networks, foundation models, LLMs)
Evaluation (e.g., methodology, meta studies, replicability and validity, human-in-the-loop)
General machine learning (supervised, unsupervised, online, active, etc.)
Infrastructure (e.g., libraries, improved implementation and scalability, distributed solutions)
Machine learning for sciences (e.g. climate, health, life sciences, physics, social sciences)
Neuroscience and cognitive science (e.g., neural coding, brain-computer interfaces)
Optimization (e.g., convex and non-convex, stochastic, robust)
Probabilistic methods (e.g., variational inference, causal inference, Gaussian processes)
Reinforcement learning (e.g., decision and control, planning, hierarchical RL, robotics)

Other (please use sparingly, only use the keyword field for more details)

Responses are confidential and will not be shared with reviewers, area chairs, or senior chairs. The PC Chairs will analyze aggregated data to understand how emerging technologies influence the research publication process. Please select all that apply below.
